PROP
40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. Supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West Opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. Trump slashed healthcare funding to pay for billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. It’s time to make billionaires pay their fair share and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
CON
Prop. 40 is a flawed, one-time tax scheme that hurts our economy, damages our state budget, and contains a loophole exposing all Californians to taxes we can’t afford—but does nothing to lower healthcare costs. No safeguards, no accountability. Join California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children’s Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Democrats and Republicans: NO on 40.

# Poll: California billionaires tax loses majority support ahead of election
## A majority of likely voters now oppose Proposition 40, while measures on voter ID and environmental review also trail
PUBLISHED: October 27, 2026 at 9:00 PM PDT | UPDATED: October 28, 2026 at 10:09 AM PDT
**Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...**
Support for a proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ wealth is waning among California voters, according to a new independent poll released this week.
Proposition 40, a highly contentious November ballot measure, has the support of 46% of likely voters in the latest survey from the Public Policy Institute of California — down from last month’s poll, which showed it had majority support with 52% of likely voters in favor.
In the latest poll, which was conducted between Oct. 16 and 22 by the San Francisco-based nonpartisan research group, 52% of likely voters were opposed and 2% were undecided.
The initiative also saw a 9-percentage-point decline in support among likely Bay Area voters, from 58% in support last month to 49% in support in the latest survey.
The PPIC surveyed 1,086 likely voters and the poll had a margin of error of 3.8 percentage points.
Proposed by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, the measure would help offset federal Medicaid cuts.

A pair of statewide measures aimed at blocking Proposition 40, Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, remained short of the needed majority support, with opposition mounting, the poll found.

Proposition 42 support remained at 43% as it was in September, while opposition rose to 45% from 34% and undecided fell to 12% from 23% last month.
Both also require majorities to pass.

PROP
40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. Supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West Opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. Trump slashed healthcare funding to pay for billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. It’s time to make billionaires pay their fair share and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
CON
Prop. 40 is a flawed, one-time tax scheme that hurts our economy, damages our state budget, and contains a loophole exposing all Californians to taxes we can’t afford—but does nothing to lower healthcare costs. No safeguards, no accountability. Join California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children’s Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Democrats and Republicans: NO on 40.

Support stood at 48% when Berkeley IGS last polled it in August, when the institute found 48% support for the billionaire tax, 41% opposed and 11% undecided.

## Poll finds proposed Proposition 40 billionaires tax losing ground since August

The poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies found 45% of likely voters in the Nov. 3 general election would support Proposition 40, the billionaires tax, less than the majority that would be needed for it to pass.
Proposition 41, backed by opponents of the billionaires tax and designed to nullify it, was backed by 37%, and another countermeasure, Proposition 42, had 43% support.
The poll found 13% were undecided on Proposition 40.
“The findings suggest tough news for Proposition 40 proponents,” said G.
Cristina Mora, co-director of the IGS poll.
“With less than 50% support this close to the election, ballot measures for new taxes tend not to pass, as undecided voters likely break towards ‘no.'”
Support stood at 48% when Berkeley IGS last polled it in August, when the institute found 48% support for the billionaire tax, 41% opposed and 11% undecided.
For two countermeasures also on the ballot, the poll found 37% in favor of Proposition 41, which would bar new state taxes that exclude revenues from a state spending limit, while 33% were opposed and 30% were undecided.

# Election 2026: Poll finds billionaire tax, counter-measures lacking majority support
## Poll finds proposed Proposition 40 billionaires tax losing ground since August
The most closely watched measure on the statewide California ballot, a tax on billionaires’ wealth, lacks majority support, as do a pair of countermeasures backed by its opponents, according to a poll published Friday.
The poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies found 45% of likely voters in the Nov. 3 general election would support Proposition 40, the billionaires tax, less than the majority that would be needed for it to pass.
Proposition 41, backed by opponents of the billionaires tax and designed to nullify it, was backed by 37%, and another countermeasure, Proposition 42, had 43% support.
The poll found 13% were undecided on Proposition 40.
“The findings suggest tough news for Proposition 40 proponents,” said G.
Cristina Mora, co-director of the IGS poll.
“With less than 50% support this close to the election, ballot measures for new taxes tend not to pass, as undecided voters likely break towards ‘no.'”
Support stood at 48% when Berkeley IGS last polled it in August, when the institute found 48% support for the billionaire tax, 41% opposed and 11% undecided.
For two countermeasures also on the ballot, the poll found 37% in favor of Proposition 41, which would bar new state taxes that exclude revenues from a state spending limit, while 33% were opposed and 30% were undecided.

Proposition 40: One-Time Wealth Tax
Proposition 40: One-Time Wealth Tax
Proposition 40: Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.
Additional Titles
The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
One-Time Wealth Tax for State-Funded Health Care Programs Initiative
Summary
Proposition 40 began as Initiative #25-0024, filed with the California Attorney General’s Office on October 22, 2025. The initiative was cleared for signature gathering on December 26, 2025, and supporters had collected at least 25% of the signatures required to qualify by February 26, 2026. They submitted signatures for verification on April 27, 2026 and the Secretary of State announced that the measure had qualified for the ballot on June 17, 2026.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on the net worth of billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026. The tax would be collected beginning in 2027, with an option to pay over five years at a higher total cost. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would not be included when calculating taxable wealth.
The state would have some discretion on how and when to spend the money from the tax, as long as 90 percent of the revenue is used to support public health care services, with the remaining funds available for education, food assistance, and costs associated with administering the tax. The money would be exempt from certain existing state constitutional spending requirements. Proposition 40 could also be prevented from taking effect if Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes and courts determine that the measures conflict.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 40 is expected to generate tens of billions of dollars in temporary state revenue over several years, although the actual amount would be uncertain because of changing asset values and actions billionaires might take to reduce their tax liability. The measure could also reduce ongoing state income tax revenue by less than $1 billion annually if some billionaires change their financial choices or leave the state. Administering and collecting the wealth tax could cost the state tens of millions of dollars each year for several years, with those expenses paid from the new tax revenue.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports a one-time 5% tax on taxable wealth above $1 billion, with the revenue primarily funding health care, as well as food assistance and public education.
No: A “no” vote opposes creating this one-time wealth tax.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 40 would require California’s wealthiest residents to contribute a modest share of their wealth to protect essential health care services, including hospitals, emergency rooms, and clinics. They contend that billionaires can afford the one-time tax, that taxing accumulated wealth is comparable to other forms of taxation such as property taxes, and that billionaire wealth has grown substantially while taxes paid relative to that wealth have remained low.
Opponents argue that Proposition 40 could encourage billionaires to leave California, reducing income tax revenue and making state finances more unpredictable. They contend that California already has high taxes and that its budget challenges stem more from spending than insufficient revenue. Proposition 40: One-Time Wealth Tax
Proposition 40: One-Time Wealth Tax
Proposition 40: Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.
Additional Titles
The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
One-Time Wealth Tax for State-Funded Health Care Programs Initiative
Summary
Proposition 40 began as Initiative #25-0024, filed with the California Attorney General’s Office on October 22, 2025. The initiative was cleared for signature gathering on December 26, 2025, and supporters had collected at least 25% of the signatures required to qualify by February 26, 2026. They submitted signatures for verification on April 27, 2026 and the Secretary of State announced that the measure had qualified for the ballot on June 17, 2026.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on the net worth of billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026. The tax would be collected beginning in 2027, with an option to pay over five years at a higher total cost. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would not be included when calculating taxable wealth.
The state would have some discretion on how and when to spend the money from the tax, as long as 90 percent of the revenue is used to support public health care services, with the remaining funds available for education, food assistance, and costs associated with administering the tax. The money would be exempt from certain existing state constitutional spending requirements. Proposition 40 could also be prevented from taking effect if Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes and courts determine that the measures conflict.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 40 is expected to generate tens of billions of dollars in temporary state revenue over several years, although the actual amount would be uncertain because of changing asset values and actions billionaires might take to reduce their tax liability. The measure could also reduce ongoing state income tax revenue by less than $1 billion annually if some billionaires change their financial choices or leave the state. Administering and collecting the wealth tax could cost the state tens of millions of dollars each year for several years, with those expenses paid from the new tax revenue.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports a one-time 5% tax on taxable wealth above $1 billion, with the revenue primarily funding health care, as well as food assistance and public education.
No: A “no” vote opposes creating this one-time wealth tax.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 40 would require California’s wealthiest residents to contribute a modest share of their wealth to protect essential health care services, including hospitals, emergency rooms, and clinics. They contend that billionaires can afford the one-time tax, that taxing accumulated wealth is comparable to other forms of taxation such as property taxes, and that billionaire wealth has grown substantially while taxes paid relative to that wealth have remained low.
Opponents argue that Proposition 40 could encourage billionaires to leave California, reducing income tax revenue and making state finances more unpredictable. They contend that California already has high taxes and that its budget challenges stem more from spending than insufficient revenue. Critics also raise concerns about unclear health care funding provisions, the measure’s potential long-term fiscal consequences, and whether wealth taxation would be more effectively addressed at the federal rather than state level.

Proposition 40: One-Time Wealth Tax
Proposition 40: One-Time Wealth Tax
Proposition 40: Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.
Additional Titles
The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
One-Time Wealth Tax for State-Funded Health Care Programs Initiative
Summary
Proposition 40 began as Initiative #25-0024, filed with the California Attorney General’s Office on October 22, 2025. The initiative was cleared for signature gathering on December 26, 2025, and supporters had collected at least 25% of the signatures required to qualify by February 26, 2026. They submitted signatures for verification on April 27, 2026 and the Secretary of State announced that the measure had qualified for the ballot on June 17, 2026.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on the net worth of billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026. The tax would be collected beginning in 2027, with an option to pay over five years at a higher total cost. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would not be included when calculating taxable wealth.
The state would have some discretion on how and when to spend the money from the tax, as long as 90 percent of the revenue is used to support public health care services, with the remaining funds available for education, food assistance, and costs associated with administering the tax. The money would be exempt from certain existing state constitutional spending requirements. Proposition 40 could also be prevented from taking effect if Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes and courts determine that the measures conflict.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 40 is expected to generate tens of billions of dollars in temporary state revenue over several years, although the actual amount would be uncertain because of changing asset values and actions billionaires might take to reduce their tax liability. The measure could also reduce ongoing state income tax revenue by less than $1 billion annually if some billionaires change their financial choices or leave the state. Administering and collecting the wealth tax could cost the state tens of millions of dollars each year for several years, with those expenses paid from the new tax revenue.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports a one-time 5% tax on taxable wealth above $1 billion, with the revenue primarily funding health care, as well as food assistance and public education.
No: A “no” vote opposes creating this one-time wealth tax.

Proposition 40: One-Time Wealth Tax
Proposition 40: One-Time Wealth Tax
Proposition 40: Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.
Additional Titles
The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
One-Time Wealth Tax for State-Funded Health Care Programs Initiative
Summary
Proposition 40 began as Initiative #25-0024, filed with the California Attorney General’s Office on October 22, 2025. The initiative was cleared for signature gathering on December 26, 2025, and supporters had collected at least 25% of the signatures required to qualify by February 26, 2026. They submitted signatures for verification on April 27, 2026 and the Secretary of State announced that the measure had qualified for the ballot on June 17, 2026.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on the net worth of billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026. The tax would be collected beginning in 2027, with an option to pay over five years at a higher total cost. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would not be included when calculating taxable wealth.
The state would have some discretion on how and when to spend the money from the tax, as long as 90 percent of the revenue is used to support public health care services, with the remaining funds available for education, food assistance, and costs associated with administering the tax. The money would be exempt from certain existing state constitutional spending requirements. Proposition 40 could also be prevented from taking effect if Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes and courts determine that the measures conflict.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 40 is expected to generate tens of billions of dollars in temporary state revenue over several years, although the actual amount would be uncertain because of changing asset values and actions billionaires might take to reduce their tax liability. The measure could also reduce ongoing state income tax revenue by less than $1 billion annually if some billionaires change their financial choices or leave the state. Administering and collecting the wealth tax could cost the state tens of millions of dollars each year for several years, with those expenses paid from the new tax revenue.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports a one-time 5% tax on taxable wealth above $1 billion, with the revenue primarily funding health care, as well as food assistance and public education.
No: A “no” vote opposes creating this one-time wealth tax.

Recent polls show that the so-called billionaire tax is losing steam among California voters.
Arguably the two most reputable pollsters of California are UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California.
Both found last month that support for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time, 5% wealth tax on California residents worth more than $1 billion, has declined, leaving neither side with a clear lead.
The results are a departure from earlier surveys by the same pollsters, which both found the "Yes" side leading the "No" in their September polls.

Polling from Berkeley IGS found a similar trend.
In October, IGS found 50% of likely voters intended to vote no on the tax, while 42% planned to vote yes, with 8% undecided.
A month earlier, just 42% planned to vote no on the tax, while 45% planned to vote yes.
Not every poll found that support for the tax is lagging.

Blog Post · November 2, 2026
Five Fast Takes on California’s Midterm Mood
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Stephanie Barton , (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Across the country and in California, Election Day is nearly upon us. More than 23.2 million Californians have registered to vote—in past election years, over 80% said they planned to vote (https://www.ppic.org/blog/who-are-californias-infrequent-voters-and-when-do-they-vote/). Californians entered the midterm in a dark mood, but has their gloom convinced them to cast their ballots? We look at the voter numbers and what issues set the mood during this election cycle.
1. The voters you might expect to vote early, did vote early. By the end of October, over 5 million registered voters (https://politicaldata.com/early-vote-counts?districtId=9999&districtName=California%20Statewide) had returned a ballot, a higher number than in the days leading up to the June primary. But ballots have arrived at a pace to be expected for a midterm. While other states across the country may have seen a surge in early voting, that bump may be due to voters who would typically vote on Election Day (https://www.npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-6012308/midterm-elections-early-voting-data).
Democratic voters have led the charge of returning ballots early, sending over 2.5 million. Republicans have returned nearly 1.5 million, and independents have sent in more than 1 million ballots. In familiar fashion, older voters and white voters have made a very strong showing—these voters constitute the bulk of early returns.
2. Young and old are eying the same gubernatorial candidate. Democrat Xavier Becerra has led in the polls since earning one of the top two spots in the governor’s race with Republican Steve Hilton. Today, Becerra claims 61% support from likely voters to Hilton’s 37% support. Over seven in ten young likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/priorities-for-californias-young-voters/) indicate they would vote for Becerra, as do well over half of voters over 50 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf). Hilton remains very popular with Republican voters, underscoring the notion that most Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) consider their candidates acceptable options.
3. The tax on billionaires has lost its appeal though the permanent tax on high earners has not. Today 46% of likely voters support Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time tax on Californians with assets over $1 billion, with fewer Democrats (64%) than a month ago (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (72%) now saying they would vote yes. Meanwhile a majority of likely voters back Proposition 3, which would extend a marginal income tax on Californians earning over $371,000. Back in September, people had grumbled about the excessive ballot measures (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/); this October, many (88%) praised the voter information guide from the Secretary of State as useful in deciding how to vote on the many initiatives.
4. Some Californians see voting as a light in the dark mood. Eighty-two percent of California adults nurse a dim view of the direction of the US, and 77% are pessimistic about California’s economic outlook. Views that housing costs are a big problem (64%), incomes are not keeping up with inflation (76%), and disapproval of US military action in Iran (75%) have further hardened attitudes.
Yet as seven in ten likely voters question the state of democracy in the US, Democratic likely voters (71%) are more enthusiastic than usual about voting for Congress, compared to 46% of Republicans. This enthusiasm comes amid new congressional districts created through redistricting that favor Democrats, where few competitive races (https://www.ppic.org/blog/the-mix-of-political-views-in-californias-new-congressional-districts/) remain among the 52 House seats up for grabs. Amid heavy disapproval of Congress (82%) and of President Trump (78%), it is no shock that 63% of likely voters intend to vote for the Democrat in their district.
5. Voters do not extend much grace to the political parties themselves, but they trust the system. In September, only 41% of likely voters felt the Democratic Party had at least some good ideas (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-0926.pdf); fewer (27%) granted the benefit of the doubt to the Republican Party. Despite this lack of faith in parties, the people still believe in the process that defines democracy: six in ten likely voters have a good deal of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections.
Although midterms have been known for their lackluster turnout, the issues and candidates this year have managed to capture the state’s attention. Voter enthusiasm and voter confidence during the 2026 election cycle may well boost the numbers at the polls.

Eighty-two percent of California adults nurse a dim view of the direction of the US, and 77% are pessimistic about California’s economic outlook. Views that housing costs are a big problem (64%), incomes are not keeping up with inflation (76%), and disapproval of US military action in Iran (75%) have further hardened attitudes.
Yet as seven in ten likely voters question the state of democracy in the US, Democratic likely voters (71%) are more enthusiastic than usual about voting for Congress, compared to 46% of Republicans. Amid heavy disapproval of Congress (82%) and of President Trump (78%), it is no shock that 63% of likely voters intend to vote for the Democrat in their district.

In September, only 41% of likely voters felt the Democratic Party had at least some good ideas (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-0926.pdf); fewer (27%) granted the benefit of the doubt to the Republican Party. Despite this lack of faith in parties, the people still believe in the process that defines democracy: six in ten likely voters have a good deal of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections.

Across the country and in California, Election Day is nearly upon us. More than 23.2 million Californians have registered to vote—in past election years, over 80% said they planned to vote (https://www.ppic.org/blog/who-are-californias-infrequent-voters-and-when-do-they-vote/). 1. The voters you might expect to vote early, did vote early. By the end of October, over 5 million registered voters (https://politicaldata.com/early-vote-counts?districtId=9999&districtName=California%20Statewide) had returned a ballot, a higher number than in the days leading up to the June primary. But ballots have arrived at a pace to be expected for a midterm. While other states across the country may have seen a surge in early voting, that bump may be due to voters who would typically vote on Election Day (https://www.npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-6012308/midterm-elections-early-voting-data).
Democratic voters have led the charge of returning ballots early, sending over 2.5 million. Republicans have returned nearly 1.5 million, and independents have sent in more than 1 million ballots. In familiar fashion, older voters and white voters have made a very strong showing—these voters constitute the bulk of early returns.
2. Young and old are eying the same gubernatorial candidate. Democrat Xavier Becerra has led in the polls since earning one of the top two spots in the governor’s race with Republican Steve Hilton. Today, Becerra claims 61% support from likely voters to Hilton’s 37% support. Over seven in ten young likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/priorities-for-californias-young-voters/) indicate they would vote for Becerra, as do well over half of voters over 50 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf). Hilton remains very popular with Republican voters, underscoring the notion that most Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) consider their candidates acceptable options.
3. The tax on billionaires has lost its appeal though the permanent tax on high earners has not. Today 46% of likely voters support Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time tax on Californians with assets over $1 billion, with fewer Democrats (64%) than a month ago (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (72%) now saying they would vote yes. Meanwhile a majority of likely voters back Proposition 3, which would extend a marginal income tax on Californians earning over $371,000. Back in September, people had grumbled about the excessive ballot measures (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/); this October, many (88%) praised the voter information guide from the Secretary of State as useful in deciding how to vote on the many initiatives.
4. Some Californians see voting as a light in the dark mood. Eighty-two percent of California adults nurse a dim view of the direction of the US, and 77% are pessimistic about California’s economic outlook. Views that housing costs are a big problem (64%), incomes are not keeping up with inflation (76%), and disapproval of US military action in Iran (75%) have further hardened attitudes.
Yet as seven in ten likely voters question the state of democracy in the US, Democratic likely voters (71%) are more enthusiastic than usual about voting for Congress, compared to 46% of Republicans. This enthusiasm comes amid new congressional districts created through redistricting that favor Democrats, where few competitive races (https://www.ppic.org/blog/the-mix-of-political-views-in-californias-new-congressional-districts/) remain among the 52 House seats up for grabs. Amid heavy disapproval of Congress (82%) and of President Trump (78%), it is no shock that 63% of likely voters intend to vote for the Democrat in their district.
5. Voters do not extend much grace to the political parties themselves, but they trust the system. In September, only 41% of likely voters felt the Democratic Party had at least some good ideas (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-0926.pdf); fewer (27%) granted the benefit of the doubt to the Republican Party. Despite this lack of faith in parties, the people still believe in the process that defines democracy: six in ten likely voters have a good deal of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections.
Although midterms have been known for their lackluster turnout, the issues and candidates this year have managed to capture the state’s attention. Voter enthusiasm and voter confidence during the 2026 election cycle may well boost the numbers at the polls.

Blog Post · November 2, 2026
Five Fast Takes on California’s Midterm Mood
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Subscribe to our blog → (https://www.ppic.org/mailing-list)
Stephanie Barton , (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/)
Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Across the country and in California, Election Day is nearly upon us. More than 23.2 million Californians have registered to vote—in past election years, over 80% said they planned to vote (https://www.ppic.org/blog/who-are-californias-infrequent-voters-and-when-do-they-vote/). Californians entered the midterm in a dark mood, but has their gloom convinced them to cast their ballots? We look at the voter numbers and what issues set the mood during this election cycle.
1. The voters you might expect to vote early, did vote early. By the end of October, over 5 million registered voters (https://politicaldata.com/early-vote-counts?districtId=9999&districtName=California%20Statewide) had returned a ballot, a higher number than in the days leading up to the June primary. But ballots have arrived at a pace to be expected for a midterm. While other states across the country may have seen a surge in early voting, that bump may be due to voters who would typically vote on Election Day (https://www.npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-6012308/midterm-elections-early-voting-data).
Democratic voters have led the charge of returning ballots early, sending over 2.5 million. Republicans have returned nearly 1.5 million, and independents have sent in more than 1 million ballots. In familiar fashion, older voters and white voters have made a very strong showing—these voters constitute the bulk of early returns.
2. Young and old are eying the same gubernatorial candidate. Democrat Xavier Becerra has led in the polls since earning one of the top two spots in the governor’s race with Republican Steve Hilton. Today, Becerra claims 61% support from likely voters to Hilton’s 37% support. Over seven in ten young likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/priorities-for-californias-young-voters/) indicate they would vote for Becerra, as do well over half of voters over 50 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf). Hilton remains very popular with Republican voters, underscoring the notion that most Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) consider their candidates acceptable options.
3. The tax on billionaires has lost its appeal though the permanent tax on high earners has not. Today 46% of likely voters support Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time tax on Californians with assets over $1 billion, with fewer Democrats (64%) than a month ago (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (72%) now saying they would vote yes. Meanwhile a majority of likely voters back Proposition 3, which would extend a marginal income tax on Californians earning over $371,000. Back in September, people had grumbled about the excessive ballot measures (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/); this October, many (88%) praised the voter information guide from the Secretary of State as useful in deciding how to vote on the many initiatives.
4. Some Californians see voting as a light in the dark mood. Eighty-two percent of California adults nurse a dim view of the direction of the US, and 77% are pessimistic about California’s economic outlook. Views that housing costs are a big problem (64%), incomes are not keeping up with inflation (76%), and disapproval of US military action in Iran (75%) have further hardened attitudes.
Yet as seven in ten likely voters question the state of democracy in the US, Democratic likely voters (71%) are more enthusiastic than usual about voting for Congress, compared to 46% of Republicans. This enthusiasm comes amid new congressional districts created through redistricting that favor Democrats, where few competitive races (https://www.ppic.org/blog/the-mix-of-political-views-in-californias-new-congressional-districts/) remain among the 52 House seats up for grabs. Amid heavy disapproval of Congress (82%) and of President Trump (78%), it is no shock that 63% of likely voters intend to vote for the Democrat in their district.
5. Voters do not extend much grace to the political parties themselves, but they trust the system. In September, only 41% of likely voters felt the Democratic Party had at least some good ideas (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-0926.pdf); fewer (27%) granted the benefit of the doubt to the Republican Party. Despite this lack of faith in parties, the people still believe in the process that defines democracy: six in ten likely voters have a good deal of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections.
Although midterms have been known for their lackluster turnout, the issues and candidates this year have managed to capture the state’s attention. Voter enthusiasm and voter confidence during the 2026 election cycle may well boost the numbers at the polls.

Wed, September 30, 2026 at 10:00 AM UTC
...
Supporters hold signs advocating for the "billionaire tax" in Los Angeles in April.
(Caroline Brehman / Bloomberg via Getty Images file)
More
A plurality of likely California voters support a proposal on the state's November ballot that would impose a one-time wealth tax on the richest Californians, but the measure is still short of majority support, according to a new NBCUniversal Local/Telemundo Station Group poll released Wednesday.
In the poll, 48% said they would vote "yes" on the proposal, while 38% said they would vote "no."
Another 14% said they were undecided.
The 10-point lead for "yes" is outside the poll's margin of error, which is plus or minus 4 percentage points for each side's support level.
The spread was almost identical among Hispanic likely voters, according to a companion survey of California: 50% said they'd vote "yes," 40% said they'd vote "no," and 10% said they were undecided.
Both surveys were conducted Sept. 21-24.

# Support dwindles for wealth tax, voter ID ballot measures, new poll shows
LOS ANGELES — California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax on billionaires' assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times.
The findings mark a significant decline in support of the measure, which was crafted by an influential California healthcare union to compensate for an estimated $100 billion in federal healthcare cuts approved by President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.

2. Where does California's Prop 40 stand? Here's what the ...
https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-polls-22503108.php
Recent polls show that the so-called billionaire tax is losing steam among California voters.
Arguably the two most reputable pollsters of California are UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California.
Both found last month that support for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time, 5% wealth tax on California residents worth more than $1 billion, has declined, leaving neither side with a clear lead.
The results are a departure from earlier surveys by the same pollsters, which both found the "Yes" side leading the "No" in their September polls.
The October poll from the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonpartisan think tank, found that 46% of likely voters said they would vote yes on the proposed tax, down from 52% in September: The numbers in opposition moved in mirror image, with the share opposing the measure growing from 46% to 52%.
Polling from Berkeley IGS found a similar trend.
In October, IGS found 50% of likely voters intended to vote no on the tax, while 42% planned to vote yes, with 8% undecided.
A month earlier, just 42% planned to vote no on the tax, while 45% planned to vote yes.
Not every poll found that support for the tax is lagging.
In early October, a Politico poll found that 46% of likely voters planned to vote Yes on Prop.
40, while 43% planned to vote no, with the rest undecided, essentially the same finding as it had a month earlier.

PROP
40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. Supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West Opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.

PRO
Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. Trump slashed healthcare funding to pay for billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. Proposition 40: One-Time Wealth Tax
Proposition 40: One-Time Wealth Tax
Proposition 40: Imposes One-Time Tax on Certain Taxpayers. Initiative Constitutional Amendment and Statute.
Additional Titles
The 2026 Billionaire Tax Act
One-Time Wealth Tax for State-Funded Health Care Programs Initiative
Summary
Proposition 40 began as Initiative #25-0024, filed with the California Attorney General’s Office on October 22, 2025. The initiative was cleared for signature gathering on December 26, 2025, and supporters had collected at least 25% of the signatures required to qualify by February 26, 2026. They submitted signatures for verification on April 27, 2026 and the Secretary of State announced that the measure had qualified for the ballot on June 17, 2026.
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on the net worth of billionaires who were California residents on January 1, 2026. The tax would be collected beginning in 2027, with an option to pay over five years at a higher total cost. Real estate, pensions, and retirement accounts generally would not be included when calculating taxable wealth.
The state would have some discretion on how and when to spend the money from the tax, as long as 90 percent of the revenue is used to support public health care services, with the remaining funds available for education, food assistance, and costs associated with administering the tax. The money would be exempt from certain existing state constitutional spending requirements. Proposition 40 could also be prevented from taking effect if Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes and courts determine that the measures conflict.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
Proposition 40 is expected to generate tens of billions of dollars in temporary state revenue over several years, although the actual amount would be uncertain because of changing asset values and actions billionaires might take to reduce their tax liability. The measure could also reduce ongoing state income tax revenue by less than $1 billion annually if some billionaires change their financial choices or leave the state. Administering and collecting the wealth tax could cost the state tens of millions of dollars each year for several years, with those expenses paid from the new tax revenue.
What your vote means
YES: A “yes” vote supports a one-time 5% tax on taxable wealth above $1 billion, with the revenue primarily funding health care, as well as food assistance and public education.
No: A “no” vote opposes creating this one-time wealth tax.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Supporters argue that Proposition 40 would require California’s wealthiest residents to contribute a modest share of their wealth to protect essential health care services, including hospitals, emergency rooms, and clinics. They contend that billionaires can afford the one-time tax, that taxing accumulated wealth is comparable to other forms of taxation such as property taxes, and that billionaire wealth has grown substantially while taxes paid relative to that wealth have remained low.
Opponents argue that Proposition 40 could encourage billionaires to leave California, reducing income tax revenue and making state finances more unpredictable. They contend that California already has high taxes and that its budget challenges stem more from spending than insufficient revenue. Critics also raise concerns about unclear health care funding provisions, the measure’s potential long-term fiscal consequences, and whether wealth taxation would be more effectively addressed at the federal rather than state level.

Stephanie Barton (https://www.ppic.org/person/stephanie-barton/) and Mark Baldassare (https://www.ppic.org/person/mark-baldassare/)
Across the country and in California, Election Day is nearly upon us. More than 23.2 million Californians have registered to vote—in past election years, over 80% said they planned to vote (https://www.ppic.org/blog/who-are-californias-infrequent-voters-and-when-do-they-vote/). Californians entered the midterm in a dark mood, but has their gloom convinced them to cast their ballots? We look at the voter numbers and what issues set the mood during this election cycle.
1. The voters you might expect to vote early, did vote early. By the end of October, over 5 million registered voters (https://politicaldata.com/early-vote-counts?districtId=9999&districtName=California%20Statewide) had returned a ballot, a higher number than in the days leading up to the June primary. But ballots have arrived at a pace to be expected for a midterm. While other states across the country may have seen a surge in early voting, that bump may be due to voters who would typically vote on Election Day (https://www.npr.org/2026/10/23/nx-s1-6012308/midterm-elections-early-voting-data).
Democratic voters have led the charge of returning ballots early, sending over 2.5 million. Republicans have returned nearly 1.5 million, and independents have sent in more than 1 million ballots. In familiar fashion, older voters and white voters have made a very strong showing—these voters constitute the bulk of early returns.
2. Young and old are eying the same gubernatorial candidate. Democrat Xavier Becerra has led in the polls since earning one of the top two spots in the governor’s race with Republican Steve Hilton. Today, Becerra claims 61% support from likely voters to Hilton’s 37% support. Over seven in ten young likely voters (https://www.ppic.org/blog/priorities-for-californias-young-voters/) indicate they would vote for Becerra, as do well over half of voters over 50 (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-likely-voters-1026.pdf). Hilton remains very popular with Republican voters, underscoring the notion that most Democrats (65%) and Republicans (67%) consider their candidates acceptable options.
3. The tax on billionaires has lost its appeal though the permanent tax on high earners has not. Today 46% of likely voters support Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time tax on Californians with assets over $1 billion, with fewer Democrats (64%) than a month ago (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) (72%) now saying they would vote yes. Meanwhile a majority of likely voters back Proposition 3, which would extend a marginal income tax on Californians earning over $371,000. Back in September, people had grumbled about the excessive ballot measures (https://www.ppic.org/blog/voters-are-displeased-by-long-ballots-and-split-on-ballot-propositions/); this October, many (88%) praised the voter information guide from the Secretary of State as useful in deciding how to vote on the many initiatives.
4. Some Californians see voting as a light in the dark mood. Eighty-two percent of California adults nurse a dim view of the direction of the US, and 77% are pessimistic about California’s economic outlook. Views that housing costs are a big problem (64%), incomes are not keeping up with inflation (76%), and disapproval of US military action in Iran (75%) have further hardened attitudes.
Yet as seven in ten likely voters question the state of democracy in the US, Democratic likely voters (71%) are more enthusiastic than usual about voting for Congress, compared to 46% of Republicans. This enthusiasm comes amid new congressional districts created through redistricting that favor Democrats, where few competitive races (https://www.ppic.org/blog/the-mix-of-political-views-in-californias-new-congressional-districts/) remain among the 52 House seats up for grabs. Amid heavy disapproval of Congress (82%) and of President Trump (78%), it is no shock that 63% of likely voters intend to vote for the Democrat in their district.
5. Voters do not extend much grace to the political parties themselves, but they trust the system. In September, only 41% of likely voters felt the Democratic Party had at least some good ideas (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/crosstabs-all-adults-0926.pdf); fewer (27%) granted the benefit of the doubt to the Republican Party. Despite this lack of faith in parties, the people still believe in the process that defines democracy: six in ten likely voters have a good deal of confidence in the system in which votes are cast and counted in California elections.
Although midterms have been known for their lackluster turnout, the issues and candidates this year have managed to capture the state’s attention. Voter enthusiasm and voter confidence during the 2026 election cycle may well boost the numbers at the polls.

Recent polls show that the so-called billionaire tax is losing steam among California voters.

Both found last month that support for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time, 5% wealth tax on California residents worth more than $1 billion, has declined, leaving neither side with a clear lead.
The results are a departure from earlier surveys by the same pollsters, which both found the "Yes" side leading the "No" in their September polls.
The October poll from the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonpartisan think tank, found that 46% of likely voters said they would vote yes on the proposed tax, down from 52% in September: The numbers in opposition moved in mirror image, with the share opposing the measure growing from 46% to 52%.
Polling from Berkeley IGS found a similar trend.
In October, IGS found 50% of likely voters intended to vote no on the tax, while 42% planned to vote yes, with 8% undecided.
